Used for entry identification, not as a substitute transcription. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

runs.text: Quem, ou quem he? quem eſtà ahi.

lines.note: Taſo is an interrogative, who or who is there. The last word is ahi, with h rather than OCR b; the entry confirms the preceding page's Taſo catchword.
Taſocare doqi denotes evening twilight. The initial is T, and the Portuguese expression reads luſco and fuſco, correcting OCR Faſocare and foſco without modernizing the Japanese form.
Taſucari is the noun salvation or deliverance. The clear initial T distinguishes the actual headword from the OCR's Faſucari.
The verb taſucari means to be saved or escape. Its intransitive force contrasts with taſuqe, saving or helping another, later in the column.
Goxǒuo taſucaru is illustrated as salvation in the next life. The lowercase example and the caron belong to the printed form; Vt is italic apparatus.
Vida completes the afterlife example. Nanguiuo taſucaru then introduces escape from danger or hardship, with its Portuguese object continuing below.
After completing de perigos, Inochiuo taſucaru means saving one's life. Preserve the printed division of Saluar between this row and the next.

Uar a vida completes the life-saving gloss. Xittçuiga taſucaru gives an expenditure-saving example; enlargement shows a short horizontal hyphen after Pou, so the divided pouparſe is recorded as Pou-/parſe.
Parſe completes pouparſe: sparing or saving expenditure. The Portuguese forrarſe supplies a second expression for economizing, not a material lining sense here.
Taſuqe is the transitive verb save or enable escape. The recipient, another person, is completed on the following physical row.
A outro completes the transitive salvation gloss, and Item adds helping as another meaning. This line clarifies the contrast with the earlier intransitive verb.
The noun Taſuqe means help or relief. Its example begins the compound Taſuqeno tçuuamono, troops sent as reinforcements, across the row boundary.
No tçuuamono completes the compound for soldiers sent in relief. The Portuguese Soldados de ſocorro confirms the military, rather than household-help, sense.

runs.text: Fita, ou corda com que atão as mãgas

lines.note: Taſuqi is a ribbon or cord for tying up sleeves. The nasal abbreviation in mãgas stands as printed; it is not a different object from mangas.
Arregaçandoas explains raising or tucking up the sleeves for work. The pronoun refers back to the sleeves, completing the definition of the fastening cord.
Taſuqe bune is a boat in which someone escapes danger. Its specific shipwreck context is completed on the following row.
Salua do naufragio specifies rescue from shipwreck. The line finishes the boat definition and does not introduce a new salvation term.
Taſuqete is defined as a saviour or deliverer. Despite resembling a modern request form, it is treated here as a person-denoting noun by the Portuguese gloss.
Tatacai is the verb to fight or contend. The worn internal t agrees with the immediately following Tatacai noun; OCR Tacacai loses that letter distinction.
The noun Tatacai means fighting, contention, or battle. Keep it separate from the preceding verb even though the same headword shape occurs.
Tatacai cutabire means to become tired from fighting. The compound and the Portuguese Canſar de pelejar express fatigue resulting from the activity.
Tatacai maqe means to be defeated in a fight. The physical pe-/leja division belongs to the Portuguese gloss and is retained.
Leja completes peleja, followed by the alternative contenda. The Latin vel is printed in full here rather than the shorter l used elsewhere.
Tatague is explicitly hair of the tanuki, Tanuqino qe. The initial is T, not OCR F; the Portuguese animal label adibe is retained without imposing a modern zoological equivalence.
Tatagueno fude names writing brushes made from this hair. Restore the visible introductory paragraph mark omitted by OCR; penas here is explained by the accompanying pinceis.
Cabelos de adibe completes the brush-material definition. The same animal name as in the headword gloss is repeated, so it should not be independently modernized.
Tatami are described as Japanese straw mattresses. The worn country name starts with I, not OCR r; retain the historical spelling Colchoens.
The verb tatami means to fold. Xiuauo ta- begins the wrinkle example, while the principal part's caron is copied as printed rather than altered from phonological expectation.
Tamu completes Xiuauo tatamu, having facial wrinkles. The next construction offers Iye or Xiro as alternative objects, a house or a fortress.
Xirouo tatamu means dismantling a fortress, alongside the preceding house alternative. The Portuguese Desfazer, not a simple folding action, supplies the sense of this application.

runs.text: leza pera ſe mudar a outra parte, &c. ¶

lines.note: Leza completes fortaleza: dismantling it to move elsewhere. The worn word reads parte, with faint t material; Ta- begins the following wave expression.
Tamu completes Tatamu nami, waves piling or folding over one another. The scan supports tamu rather than the OCR tamiu; the Portuguese describes their violent movement.
Como encapelladas further describes the waves as heaped or crested. This continuation belongs to the wave example, not to the masonry verb below.
Tatami ague means to build up or lay stones. The worn vowel before gue is a, not OCR z; the following aguru example confirms the verb family.
The stones are set in a building, followed by Ixiuo ta- as the example's beginning. Preserve the source's aß spelling and the physical Japanese word division.
Tami aguru completes Ixiuo tatami aguru, building up the stones. The short Japanese-only continuation is not an independent headword and needs no inserted translation.
Tatami bǒchǒ names a mat-maker's cutting knife. The damaged second t of Tatami is recoverable from residual strokes; both visible o-marks are carons and remain so.

runs.text: q̃ os oficiaes de Tatamis cortão as eſteiras, &c.

lines.note: The knife is used by tatami makers to cut the mats. Tatamis is embedded in Portuguese and is italic: its sloping, single-storey a and narrow m contrast with the nearby upright headword types. Preserve the abbreviation q̃ and the Portuguese plural ending.
Tatami caſane means folding with multiple folds or layers. The caſane element contributes repetition or layering, which the Portuguese expands across the line boundary.
Tas completes muitas dobras, many folds. This short Portuguese-only row is the continuation of the folding compound, not part of the next noun.
Tatami donſu is glossed literally as pieces of brick or tile. Preserve that supplied definition without substituting a textile gloss suggested by the familiar word donsu.

Tatami ſaxi denotes the person who makes tatami. The embedded Tatamis belongs to the italic Portuguese gloss; second-pass comparison with upright headwords corrects the first-pass font separation without changing the word.

runs.text: Eſteira que ſe dobra polo me-

lines.note: Tatami muxiro is a mat that can be folded in half. The Portuguese me- begins meyo, its middle, on the next physical row.
Yo completes meyo ao comprido, specifying a lengthwise fold. This detail distinguishes the object from an unspecified folding mat.
Tatami macura names folding wooden headrests or pillows. The historical almofadas wording is retained rather than replaced with a modern furniture label.
Ças completes dobradiças, folding or hinged; the objects are likened to stands. Preserve the grave accent in à and the source's comparison.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de catre, ou ban-

lines.note: Tatamino dai is a kind of frame or workbench for tatami. The damaged but readable headword replaces the garbled OCR ſaianuino; ban- continues as banca at the top of column 2.
The second running header visibly omits N from ANTES. Retain the printed ATES; the adjoining 242. is separated into the page-number zone without losing either component.

runs.text: ca ſobre que poem, & fazem Tatamis.

lines.note: Ca completes banca from column 1: the workbench on which tatami are placed and made. The embedded noun reads Tatamis, not OCR Taramis, and is marked for word-level typeface review.

runs.text: Caſa onde fazem, ou vendem Ta-

lines.note: Tatamiya can mean the place where tatami are made or sold. The embedded Ta- is the start of the Portuguese-pluralized Japanese term Tatamis, divided into the next row.
Tamis completes the embedded Tatamis; the gloss also allows the person who makes them. Preserve the printed continuous osfaz rather than inserting an expected modern space.
Tatan and Tatanna are explained by Vouoi as many in number. The Japanese synonym is separate from the Portuguese explanation and is not an embedded-term font candidate.
Quantidade completes many in quantity. It is a short continuation of the preceding quantity adjective, not a separate abstract noun entry.
Tataqi means to strike or deliver blows. Its principal parts identify the verb used in the two imperatives or examples that follow.
Ano yatçuuo tataqe is an order to strike that fellow. Restore the omitted paragraph mark; the Portuguese ma- begins madraço on the next row.
Draço completes madraço in the command to beat the fellow. Monuo tataqu introduces the distinct example of knocking on a door.
Bater à porta translates Monuo tataqu. The grave accent on à is visible and is retained rather than normalized or dropped.
Tataqi ai describes exchanging blows. The reciprocal sense is explicit in the Portuguese explanation continued below, not merely striking a single object.

runs.text: darſe de pancadas hũ a outro.

lines.note: Darſe de pancadas hũ a outro explains the mutual beating. The abbreviation hũ remains unexpanded and is followed by the separate preposition a.
Tataqi comi means to drive something inward by beating or hammering. The final principal part carries a circumflex, unlike the nearby caroned o forms.
Dentro como pregos specifies driving things inward, with nails as the example. This completes the preceding hammering compound rather than defining a separate tool.
Tataqi coroxi means to beat to death. The nasalized spelling pẽcadas is retained as printed instead of being silently changed to modern pancadas.

runs.text: Fornalha em que fazem ferro de area,

lines.note: Tatara is a furnace for making iron from sand. The Portuguese definition names the furnace, not merely the bellows that may be associated with the word elsewhere.

runs.text: ou fundem panelas de cobre, ou ferro.

lines.note: The same furnace is also used to cast copper or iron pots. This second industrial use belongs to the Tatara definition.
Tatari is equated with Bachi, punishment, and described as a supernatural affliction. The agents responsible are listed on the next line.

runs.text: Camis, & Fotoques, ou o diabo faz a alguẽ.

lines.note: The historical gloss attributes the affliction to Camis, Fotoques, or the devil. Camis and Fotoques are Japanese religious terms embedded in Portuguese; retain the source's missionary framing rather than asserting it as fact.

runs.text: Cami. l, Fotoqe. l, Tenguno tata-

lines.note: Cami, Fotoqe, and Tengu are alternative agents in the Japanese tatari example. These are standalone Japanese examples, not embedded Portuguese terms for font toggling.

runs.text: He caſtigo dos Camis, ou Fotoques,

lines.note: Rigia completes the tatari example, followed by the Portuguese explanation of punishment by Camis or Fotoques. The two pluralized religious names are embedded in the Portuguese sentence here.
Ou vexação do diabo completes the historical translation of the supernatural affliction example. It should not be merged into the next verb's ordinary harmful-effect sense.
Tatari is now the verb for something having a harmful effect. Preserve the source's abbreviated principal part u and atta rather than regularizing them from a modern verb paradigm.
Coreua facuchǔni tataru is glossed as this being bad for the stomach. Preserve the visibly printed facuchǔni, including its a, rather than forcing an expected modern Japanese form.
Eſtamago completes the bodily-harm example. Camiga tatararuru begins the divine-affliction example, with the historical honorific-looking verb form retained exactly.

runs.text: zer o Cami mal, ou vexar a alguem.

lines.note: Zer completes Fazer: a Cami causes harm or afflicts someone. Cami is embedded in a Portuguese sentence here, unlike the standalone Japanese example on the preceding line.
Tataye means to overflow or fill to overflowing. The gloss visibly contains b in Treſbordar; Xiuoga begins the example of the tide reaching its fullness.

runs.text: Eſtar a marè chea ou ſer preamar.

lines.note: Tatayuru completes the tide example, explained as full tide or high water. Preserve marè with its printed grave accent and the separate preamar paraphrase.
The dictionary explicitly says the verb also governs an accusative object. Mizzu- starts the transitive example that illustrates this grammatical qualification.
Uo completes Mizzuuo, filling with water until overflowing. The preposition is atè, not OCR arè; retain the source's short s in tresbordar rather than globally harmonizing it.
The second transitive example fills a vessel with sake. Restore the visible paragraph mark before Vtçuuamononi; the Portuguese translation begins Encher across the row boundary.

runs.text: cher o vaſo de vinho atè treſbordar.

lines.note: Cher completes Encher, filling the vessel with wine until it overflows. Vinho is the historical Portuguese rendering of sake here, not evidence of a different Japanese drink word.
Tatazumai is a condition or manner of living. The paired Portuguese expressions continue into the next row and define the broader situation, not only physical posture.
After completing the life-description gloss, Miyacono tatazumai introduces living in the capital. The repeated word reads tatazumai, not OCR tarazumai; the terminal hyphen remains.

runs.text: O estado, ou modo de viuer no

lines.note: Ga narumai completes the negative prospective statement that such a way of living will not be possible. The Portuguese wording continues its location into Miyaco below.
Miyaco supplies the capital as the location in the Portuguese sentence and is an embedded term. Iyeno tatazu- then begins the example referring to a house or dwelling.

runs.text: Modo, ou maneira da morar, ou ha-

lines.note: Mai completes Iyeno tatazumai. Enlargement shows da in maneira da morar, with the same a-form as maneira; retain this printed grammatical anomaly rather than silently substituting expected de. Ha- begins habitação on the next row.
Bitação completes habitação, dwelling or habitation. This row closes the Tatazumai entry and must remain a separate physical line.
Tatazumi means to remain suspended or undecided. The caroned-u principal part is retained, and the explanation of inaction continues below.
The person remains undecided, doing nothing. The scan gives continuous indeterminado, correcting the spurious OCR space in indetermina do.
Tatazumi aruqi means walking about in an uncertain or aimless state. The printed qu and uita principal parts are retained rather than modernized.
Rias completes varias partes: moving through different places while undecided or suspended. The wording finishes the compound's manner-of-motion gloss.

runs.text: Ermidas, ou cellas de cada Bonzo

lines.note: Tatchǔ denotes hermitages or individual monks' cells. The explanation locates them within the larger religious establishment on the following rows.

runs.text: que estão dentro do circuito dalgũa Tera prin-

lines.note: The cells are within the precinct of a principal temple. The visible words dentro and circuito replace garbled OCR; Tera is embedded in the Portuguese explanation, and dalgũa retains its printed tilde.
Cipal completes principal, qualifying the larger temple. The short row belongs to the temple-cell description, not to Tatçu below.
Tatçu is glossed Lagarto, literally a lizard. Preserve that historical gloss rather than silently substituting the modern English referent dragon suggested by tatsu.

runs.text: Nome de hum como ſigno celeste com

lines.note: A second Tatçu entry describes one of the signs used in reckoning time. Nome has no secure tilde: the apparent mark in the cropped preview belongs to the descending g of Lagarto in the preceding row. The following lines explain the sign's calendrical function.

runs.text: outros que os Iapões tomão pera contar os an-

lines.note: The Japanese are said to use these signs to count years. Tomão includes the final o omitted by OCR; an- continues as nos on the next page, also anticipated by the catchword.
The signature consists of capital P followed by two lowercase p types and the number 2. It is separate from the italic catchword nos at the far right.
This italic catchword anticipates nos at the top of f476, completing an-/nos. The separate gathering signature formerly merged into this line is retained as sig-l001.
